title: Classification Accuracy
subtitle: Topic: Classification Accuracy · Subject: AI Evaluation and Benchmarking. Three beginner, two medium and two advanced questions, seven original SVG figures and balanced teaching choices, with a tested 15-line scikit-learn example.
hero:
CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY · VISUAL STUDY

How often did the classifier make the right decision?

Classification accuracy measures the fraction of examples with correct predicted labels. It is a natural starting point—but skewed classes, decision thresholds, group disparities and multilabel outputs all affect how meaningful it is.

questions.stem: What is Classification Accuracy in Machine Learning, and how is it calculated from correct and incorrect predictions?
options: Classification accuracy measures the share of predicted positive examples that are truly positive. It divides true positives by true positives plus false positives, ignoring all correct predictions of the negative class.

Classification accuracy measures how many actual positive cases were found, so it divides true positives by true positives plus false negatives. It deliberately ignores the model's correct negative predictions and false alarms.
Accuracy is the share of correctly labeled examples: (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN). With 33 true positives and 52 true negatives among 100 cases, accuracy is 85%, counting both classes.

Classification accuracy calculates the arithmetic mean of precision and recall, so correct negative predictions contribute only indirectly. The result always equals F1 whenever there are both positive and negative labels.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Accuracy asks how often a classifier's predicted label matches the true label. For binary classification, both correctly recognized positives and correctly rejected negatives count: accuracy=(TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN). In the example, 33 true positives plus 52 true negatives give 85 correct predictions out of 100, or 85%. Nine false alarms and six missed positives are the remaining errors. For a document-sorting classifier, this summarizes correct category choices but does not reveal which kind of mistake causes more harm.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 01 · CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY

Measure correct predictions across both classes

With true negatives 52 and true positives 33 out of 100 examples, accuracy is (52+33)/100=85%. False positives 9 and false negatives 6 make up the 15 errors.

questions.stem: Why can Classification Accuracy be misleading on an imbalanced dataset, such as a rare-fraud problem with 95 negative transactions and only five positive transactions?
options: A classifier predicting every transaction negative achieves 95% accuracy but detects none of the five positives. Its positive recall is 0%, and its balanced accuracy is 50%, so accuracy alone hides the failure.

A classifier predicting every transaction negative must score only 50% accuracy because binary tasks always weight positive and negative classes equally. The five positive examples therefore have the same total weight as ninety-five negatives.

Class imbalance affects only probability calibration and cannot change the meaning of classification accuracy. A model that predicts every transaction negative is considered reliable if its reported accuracy exceeds ninety percent.

An always-negative classifier has perfect positive-class recall because it never creates false alarms, so its 95% accuracy correctly shows excellent fraud detection. Precision and balanced accuracy would report the same value.
questions.explanation: Explanation: When one class dominates a dataset, a model can be correct frequently by always selecting the majority class. If 95 of 100 transactions are legitimate, labeling everything legitimate yields 95% accuracy while missing every fraudulent transaction. Positive recall is 0%, and balanced accuracy is 50% because it averages recall over the two classes: 100% for negatives and 0% for positives. For fraud prevention or equipment failure detection, report confusion counts, class-specific recall, precision and error costs alongside accuracy.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 02 · CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY

Why 95% accuracy can still miss every fraud

In a dataset with 95 negatives and five positives, predicting every example negative yields 95% accuracy, zero positive recall and 50% balanced accuracy.

questions.stem: How can changing a binary decision threshold affect Classification Accuracy and minority-class recall, even though the learned model scores and true labels remain unchanged?
options: Raising the score threshold always improves both overall accuracy and positive recall, because the classifier makes fewer false alarms without ever losing a true positive. Rechecking the confusion matrix is therefore unnecessary.

Changing a classification threshold changes the ground-truth labels assigned to examples, which is why accuracy can rise. Positive-class recall stays constant because the actual number of positive records is fixed.

Accuracy is calculated directly from unthresholded probabilities, so changing a threshold cannot alter it. Only precision changes when predicted positive labels are assigned using a new operating point.
Changing the threshold shifts which scores count as positive, altering TP, TN, FP and FN. Here accuracy rises from 88.0% to 90.7%, while positive recall falls from 60% to 30%.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A decision threshold converts model scores into predicted class labels. Raising it can remove false alarms, adding true negatives, but can also miss positives, adding false negatives. The demonstrated 75-case holdout starts with 88.0% accuracy and 60% positive recall at threshold 0.20. At 0.80, accuracy reaches 90.7% while positive recall falls to 30%. This can happen when the negative class is more common. A safety-alert system should choose its threshold using validation data and the real costs of misses.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 03 · CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY

A higher threshold can improve accuracy but miss positives

On a tested 75-case holdout, accuracy increases from 88.0% at threshold 0.20 to 90.7% at 0.80, while positive recall falls from 60% to 30%.

questions.tag: Medium · Multiclass diagonal and class recall
questions.stem: How is Classification Accuracy computed from a multiclass confusion matrix, and why should per-class recall be inspected even when the overall accuracy is reasonably high?
options: Multiclass accuracy equals the average probability of the most likely class rather than the number of correct labels. The confusion-matrix diagonal estimates confidence, while row totals measure the number of predicted examples.

Multiclass accuracy divides the confusion-matrix diagonal sum by all examples. Here (25+14+7)/60 is 76.7%, but class C recall is only 7/12≈58.3%, revealing that overall accuracy hides errors in a particular class.

Multiclass accuracy divides each class's correct count by its predicted column total, then averages the resulting precisions. This means classes with low recall cannot reduce accuracy when other classes are frequent.

Multiclass accuracy counts every off-diagonal cell as a partial success because the model still selected a valid class. Only examples assigned no class count as errors, so accuracy cannot be derived from the diagonal alone.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A multiclass confusion matrix has true classes on rows and predicted classes on columns. Diagonal entries are correct predictions. For the illustrated 60-case example, 25+14+7=46 examples are correctly classified, producing accuracy 46/60≈76.7%. Class C has twelve actual cases but only seven recognized, so its recall is 7/12≈58.3%. A wildlife-species classifier might perform well overall yet miss a less common protected species. Reporting the matrix and class-specific metrics makes these failures visible.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 04 · CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY

Read the diagonal — then inspect each class

For 60 single-label cases, diagonal counts 25, 14 and 7 give 46 correct, or 76.7% accuracy. Class C recall is only 7/12≈58.3%.

questions.tag: Medium · Leakage-free sklearn accuracy and balanced accuracy
questions.stem: How should Classification Accuracy be evaluated with scikit-learn on a held-out dataset, and what does balanced_accuracy_score reveal beyond ordinary accuracy on imbalanced examples?
options: Fit StandardScaler on the entire dataset before splitting, then train LogisticRegression on the training portion. Choose whichever decision threshold maximizes test accuracy and report that same test score as an unbiased final estimate.

Treat every predicted positive probability above zero as correct and use mean_squared_error to report accuracy. Balanced accuracy is the difference between predicted probabilities and actual labels rather than a class-based metric.

Split labeled cases before fitting, use a training pipeline for StandardScaler and LogisticRegression, and compare held-out accuracy_score with balanced_accuracy_score, the mean of class recalls. Avoid fitting preprocessing on test examples.

Train separate classifiers for the majority and minority classes using the held-out labels, then combine their highest accuracies. Balanced accuracy can only be computed after oversampling the test set to equalize class counts.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The reproducible example first divides 300 labeled samples into 225 training and 75 test cases. A Pipeline fits StandardScaler and LogisticRegression using only training data. The held-out labels are compared with thresholded predictions using accuracy_score and balanced_accuracy_score. Balanced accuracy averages recall across classes, so the minority class has equal influence in the average. As the demonstration threshold rises, ordinary accuracy increases from 0.880 to 0.907 while balanced accuracy drops from 0.762 to 0.650. Do not tune a final threshold using test outcomes.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 05 · CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY

Fit on training data; evaluate on held-out data

scikit-learn · Accuracy, balanced accuracy and recall 15 lines
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, accuracy_score, balanced_accuracy_score, recall_score
X,y=make_classification(n_samples=300,n_features=6,n_informative=4,
    n_redundant=0,weights=[.88,.12],flip_y=.025,class_sep=.85,random_state=19)
Xtr,Xte,ytr,yte=train_test_split(X,y,test_size=.25,stratify=y,random_state=7)
model=make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),LogisticRegression(max_iter=500)).fit(Xtr,ytr)
scores=model.predict_proba(Xte)[:,1]
for threshold in (.2,.5,.8):
    pred=(scores>=threshold).astype(int)
    tn,fp,fn,tp=confusion_matrix(yte,pred).ravel()
    print(threshold,(tn,fp,fn,tp),round(accuracy_score(yte,pred),3),round(balanced_accuracy_score(yte,pred),3),round(recall_score(yte,pred),3))

The tested 15-line pipeline evaluates 75 held-out cases. Accuracy goes from 0.880 to 0.907 as the threshold rises, but balanced accuracy falls from 0.762 to 0.650.

questions.stem: How can overall Classification Accuracy conceal unequal performance across demographic, geographic or operational groups, and what additional reporting gives a more reliable comparison?
options: Overall accuracy hides weaker groups when large groups dominate: group A scores 81/90 and group B 3/10, producing 84% overall. Report subgroup accuracies, sizes and class-specific errors.

Overall accuracy automatically weights each subgroup equally, so its value must match the arithmetic mean of subgroup accuracies. A group with fewer test examples cannot affect the result differently from larger groups.

A classifier's accuracy is identical across subgroups whenever it uses the same set of input features. Different subgroup results are caused only by differing confidence thresholds and disappear when probabilities are calibrated.

Subgroup accuracy can be interpreted without knowing sample sizes or label prevalence because all groups share the same target distribution. Reporting global accuracy alone therefore provides a complete comparison of deployment outcomes.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Overall accuracy counts every evaluated example, so a large subgroup can dominate the aggregate. In the illustrated benchmark, group A has 81 correct of 90 cases, or 90%, while group B has three correct of ten, or 30%. Combined accuracy is 84%, which obscures the second group's weak result. An equal-weight average of the two group accuracies is 60%. For a multilingual support classifier, report subgroup sample sizes, class composition, uncertainty and class-specific errors; small groups can produce noisy estimates.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 06 · CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY

Overall 84% can conceal a group scoring 30%

Group A has 81/90=90% accuracy; group B has 3/10=30%. Combined accuracy is 84%, while the equal-weight mean of the two group accuracies is 60%.

questions.tag: Advanced · Top-k versus exact-match multilabel accuracy
questions.stem: Why do top-k Classification Accuracy and multilabel exact-match accuracy measure different kinds of correctness, and what reporting precautions matter for AI benchmarks?
options: Top-k accuracy requires every possible label to be correct simultaneously, while multilabel exact-match accuracy accepts any one correct tag. They are equivalent whenever the classifier outputs scores for multiple categories.

Top-k accuracy is computed by summing all class probabilities rather than comparing predicted and true labels. Multilabel accuracy instead measures only the number of correct negative tags in each example.

Top-k accuracy and multilabel subset accuracy both treat every extra predicted label as acceptable, so adding more labels or increasing k can never change a previously correct prediction into an error.

Top-k accuracy counts a correct class when it is among the k highest-ranked choices. Multilabel exact-match requires every predicted label to match. Benchmarks must state k, label order and task type.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Top-k accuracy belongs to tasks with one correct class among several choices. A prediction counts as correct if that class appears within the k highest-scoring labels. In the diagram, top-1 accuracy is 2/4=50%, while top-2 accuracy is 3/4=75%. Multilabel classification allows several true labels, and scikit-learn's accuracy_score uses strict subset accuracy: every predicted tag must match. For example, predicting [1,1,1] for true [1,0,1] is wrong. Benchmarks should explicitly identify the task, label order, k and averaging convention.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 07 · CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY

Top-k shortlists and exact-match label sets

For four exclusive-label examples, top-1 accuracy is 2/4=50% and top-2 accuracy 3/4=75%. In multilabel subset accuracy, one extra predicted tag makes the sample incorrect.
